questions.scoringGuide: AP Chemistry Q1 (Long Answer), 10 points, one point per part. Topic: magnesium isotopes, Coulombic attraction, and Mg(OH)2 solubility. A(i) [Pt1]: plot two mass-spectrum lines for Mg-25 and Mg-26 with relative abundance between 10 and 11. A(ii) [Pt2]: Mg-26 has one more neutron than Mg-25. B(i) [Pt3]: Na+ has a smaller charge than Mg2+, so weaker Coulombic attraction to water. B(ii) [Pt4]: Na+ is larger than Mg2+, so greater ion–water distance and weaker attraction (must reference interparticle distance, not nuclear pull). C [Pt5]: pOH = −log(2.80×10^−4)=3.553, pH=10.447. D [Pt6]: dilution M1V1=M2V2 to get [Mg2+]=7.62×10^−4 M after mixing (uses final combined volume). E(i) [Pt7]: Ksp=[Mg2+][OH−]^2 (OH− squared, correct charges). E(ii) [Pt8]: Q=[Mg2+][OH−]^2=2.07×10^−11, consistent with D. E(iii) [Pt9]: Q>Ksp so a precipitate forms. F [Pt10]: adding HNO3 decreases [OH−] making Q<Ksp, so more Mg(OH)2 dissolves (less solid). Common failure: forgetting to square [OH−], using initial volume in dilution, and attributing F to a common-ion or direct acid–solid reaction.

questions.scoringGuide: AP Chemistry Q3 (Long Answer), 10 points, one point per part. Topic: phosphorus oxides — Lewis structure, thermodynamics, calorimetry, Hess's law, and equilibrium. A [Pt1]: correct Lewis diagram (two lone-pair electrons on each P atom). B(i) [Pt2]: entropy decreases because gaseous reactants have more microstates/dispersal than the solid product (particle-level reasoning required). B(ii) [Pt3]: using ΔG°=ΔH°−TΔS°, the reaction is favorable because it is exothermic (ΔH°<0 drives favorability; ΔS°<0 does not). C(i) [Pt4]: q=mcΔT (≈0.16 kJ) reported to correct sig figs (two). C(ii) [Pt5]: ΔH°rxn magnitude per mole (≈450 kJ/mol) consistent with C(i); [Pt6]: correct negative sign (exothermic). D [Pt7]: with less P4O10, ΔT is 'less than' because less thermal energy is transferred. E [Pt8]: ΔHf via Hess's law (−375 kJ/mol). F(i) [Pt9]: Kp from partial pressures read off the particle diagram (=0.333); F(ii) [Pt10]: Kp decreases with higher T because the exothermic reaction favors reactants. Common failure: significant-figure errors (C(i)), dividing q by coefficients instead of moles of P4O10 (C(ii)), and temperature/equilibrium reasoning errors in D and F(ii).

questions.scoringGuide: AP Chemistry Q6 (Short Answer), 4 points, one per part. Topic: electrochemistry (Al/Zn galvanic cell). A [Pt1]: oxidation half-reaction Al → Al3+ + 3e−. B [Pt2]: balanced net ionic equation 2 Al + 3 Zn2+ → 2 Al3+ + 3 Zn. C [Pt3]: Zn experiences the greater mass change — must justify with molar masses AND stoichiometry (for every ~54 g Al consumed, ~196 g Zn is produced; a mole ratio alone is insufficient). D [Pt4]: calculate the maximum cell potential from the table (Zn oxidized, Au3+ reduced): E°cell = 1.50 + 0.76 = 2.26 V. questions.scoringGuide: AP Chemistry Q7 (Short Answer), 4 points, one per part. Topic: glycolate ion (acid–base) and a reaction mechanism. A [Pt1]: circle a correct oxygen atom (either of the two equivalent resonance C–O bonds on the carboxylate is acceptable). B(i) [Pt2]: calculate Kb = [HAsc-analog][OH−]/[conjugate base] ≈ 6.8×10^−11 by substituting the correct concentrations. B(ii) [Pt3]: calculate Ka from Kw = Ka·Kb (Ka = 1.0×10^−14 / 6.8×10^−11 = 1.5×10^−4), consistent with B(i). C [Pt4]: agree that H3O+ acts as a catalyst — consumed in step 1 and regenerated in step 2, so it is not in the overall reaction. Common failure: circling a carbon rather than oxygen; using Ka = 1/Kb instead of Kw/Kb; agreeing in C without a mechanism-based justification.
